claims.text: Elevated-temperature stress–strain behavior in HfNbTaTiZr is explained by thermally activated dislocation motion and changes in elastic anisotropy.
Elevated-temperature thermal expansion in HfNbTaTiZr is explained by thermally activated dislocation motion and changes in elastic anisotropy.
Elevated-temperature elastic behavior in HfNbTaTiZr is explained by thermally activated dislocation motion and changes in elastic anisotropy.
The initial material may be a single-phase solid solution.
Temperature-dependent behavior will be investigated using in situ neutron diffraction and first-principles calculations.
Room temperature, specified as 20°C or 293 K, is the baseline state.
Dislocation density and distribution are the structural mediator.
Thermally activated dislocation motion results in changes in elastic anisotropy.
At 800°C (1073 K), yield strength will be 20% higher than at room temperature.
At 800°C (1073 K), the thermal expansion coefficient will be 15% lower than at room temperature.
The hypothesis is intended to hold from 500°C to 1000°C and at strain rates from 10^-4 s^-1 to 10^-2 s^-1.
Interactions between dislocation mechanisms and the alloy microstructure may alter the predicted response.
The hypothesis is falsified if, at 800°C, yield strength fails to increase by at least 10% and the thermal expansion coefficient fails to decrease by at least 5% relative to room temperature.

contradictions.description: The Celsius and kelvin limits are presented as equivalent, but 500–1000°C converts to approximately 773–1273 K rather than 800–1300 K.
